name: Aaron Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and anything you say is confidential. Feel free to give me the public answer and the private one. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends what's ringing. We grow sugar beet and barley on about two hundred and forty hectares, and we buy in lambs in autumn and finish them on the beet tops over winter, that's fattening them up for market. Then there's the contracting side: my son Josh and I go round neighbours doing hedge-cutting, baling and drilling with our own kit. Most mornings I'm in the truck by seven with the AI assistant on the phone sorting the day's jobs and checking the barley price, and Josh is already out on the hedge-cutter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a good deal. Selling barley at the top of the market, or winning a contract off a bigger firm. What wears me out is the waiting: for weather, for the beet factory to give us a delivery slot, for the government to decide what this year's rules are. I've used AI tools every day for about three years now, and it's made the business side twice as easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, the tools are still handy. I'd probably post on the contractors' forum that the hype's over and it's back to who works hardest. That's always been how it is anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a touch disappointed. I'd been eyeing a robot hedge-cutter like a lad eyes a sports car. But the contracting would carry on fine, so no harm done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd still buy a new baler next summer, about forty-five thousand, partly on finance, because the contracting work's growing. I'd keep the AI for pricing and booking jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ruth, your wife, make of all your gadgets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's the school secretary in the village and runs the Sunday school. She says I treat machines the way other men treat golf. She's not wrong, but golf doesn't pay for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be glad in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older men in chapel, mostly. Some of them think AI is the work of the devil, and I don't argue with them on a Sunday. Monday, I'm back on the phone with it.

S0.say: The tools are still handy, so fair enough. The hype's over and it's back to who works hardest, which is how it's always been.
S0.think: I'd be a touch disappointed, because I'd been eyeing a robot hedge-cutter like a lad eyes a sports car. The contracting would carry on fine, so no harm done.
S0.do: Keeps going as now and buys a new baler next summer for about forty-five thousand, partly on finance, to grow the contracting work. Keeps using AI daily for pricing and job booking.
S0.quote: I'd been eyeing a robot hedge-cutter like a lad eyes a sports car.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is a businessman as much as a farmer, with a contracting side run with his son Josh. He's chapel-going and traditional on family, but sees no conflict with daily AI use, and he doesn't argue with older members who distrust it. His appetite for machinery is almost playful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work. Every new machine needs someone to run it, sell it, fix it and hire it out. I'd say people shouldn't wait for the government to save them, they should get stuck in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's an opportunity for us. Most farmers round here won't buy a robot for themselves. They'll ring someone who has one, and I want that someone to be Josh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a robot weeder and a self-steering sprayer in the first year, about a hundred thousand, half savings, half finance. I'd set Josh up running a robot contracting service for the smaller farms. And I'd get both of us on the dealer's training course so we can do our own repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and excited. Like the first day of harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A hundred thousand is a lot to put in at fifty-eight. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. We've got well over a year's costs in savings and the land behind us. If it goes wrong, I've lost some money, not the farm. And Josh is thirty, he's got the years to pay it off if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out from your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bigger contracting firm in town, Harlow's, probably. And their drivers. I'd feel for the drivers, but that's business. If they're good, I'd hire one of them.

S1.say: This is a chance for anyone willing to work. Every new machine needs someone to run, sell, fix and hire it out, so people should get stuck in rather than wait for government.
S1.think: It's an opportunity for us. Most farmers won't buy a robot themselves; they'll ring someone who has one, and I want that to be Josh.
S1.do: Buys a robot weeder and self-steering sprayer for about a hundred thousand, half from savings and half on finance. Sets his son up running a robot contracting service and gets them both on the dealer's repair course.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like the first day of harvest.
S1.quote: Most farmers round here won't buy a robot for themselves. They'll ring someone who has one, and I want that someone to be Josh.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron sees robots as a contracting opportunity: neighbours will hire rather than buy. He is comfortable taking on finance at fifty-eight because the land and savings cap his downside. He was frank that a rival firm's drivers would lose out, and offered to hire the good ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's make it much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the ones who move first will do best, and I'd say it on the forum and at the market. I'd also say families should stick together and help each other through it. I wouldn't call for handouts, I'd call for people to get to work on the new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd do all right, maybe better than all right. The contracting with robots would be in huge demand for a year or two. In two years, every farm round here either buys a robot or rings us. I'd rather be the phone that rings. The only thing I'd worry about is after that, when the robots get cheap enough that everyone has their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move in the first three months: buy as many robots as the savings and the bank would allow, maybe two hundred thousand. I'd hire one or two of the best drivers from Harlow's before they're laid off and train them up. And I'd sit down with Ruth and the family to agree that we sell the contracting business by about 2031, while it's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little flutter in the stomach, like before an auction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families should stick together. What would that mean for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josh comes in as a full partner straight away. Hannah's a vet nurse, and if robots start doing that, she comes home and does our books and the lambs. Ruth and I would want everyone close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calm. Is there anything that would actually frighten you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chapel, maybe. Half the congregation are older farmers who won't adapt, and some of them are friends. I'd hate to see them sell up for nothing. I'd offer them our services at cost, but I can't make them take it.

S2.say: The ones who move first will do best, and families should stick together and help each other through. People should get to work on the new things, not wait for handouts.
S2.think: We'd do all right, maybe better. Every farm round here either buys a robot or rings us, and I'd rather be the phone that rings, though the boom won't last once robots get cheap.
S2.do: Spends up to two hundred thousand on robots within three months, using savings and the bank. Hires the best drivers from a rival firm before they're laid off and agrees with his family to sell the contracting business by about 2031.
S2.feel: Mostly calm, with a flutter like before an auction.
S2.quote: In two years, every farm round here either buys a robot or rings us. I'd rather be the phone that rings.
S2.fieldNote: Even at two years Aaron stays calm, because his land and savings cap the downside and he sees a short boom in robot contracting. He already plans the exit, selling by 2031 before robots get cheap. His only real worry is older chapel friends who won't adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone with get-up-and-go. Learn the machines, start a business, help your neighbours. I'd tell young people to take apprenticeships with the dealers and repair firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's my favourite of the lot. Five years is long enough to build something and sell it before the big boys catch up. I'd be sixty-three when it lands, which is about when I'd want to hand over to Josh anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy machines in steps, two a year, each paid off before the next. I'd take on an apprentice from the dealer's scheme. And I'd plan for Josh to buy me out of the contracting side by 2031, with me keeping the farm and the lambs to potter with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Properly calm, the way you feel when you've got a good plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this compare with the two-year one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm gambling with borrowed money and hoping I sell in time. Five years, I'm building with my own money and choosing when to sell. Same robots, a lot less risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the older men at chapel this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you've got five years, get your son or daughter on a course, or rent your land to someone who'll use the machines. Don't sell to the investment funds. Keep it in families. They'd listen to that more than to me talking about robots.

S3.say: Five years is a gift for anyone with get-up-and-go: learn the machines, start a business, help your neighbours. Young people should take apprenticeships with the dealers and repair firms.
S3.think: It's my favourite of the lot. Five years is long enough to build something and sell it before the big firms catch up, and I'd be sixty-three, about when I'd hand over anyway.
S3.do: Buys two machines a year, each paid off before the next, and takes on an apprentice from the dealer's scheme. Plans for Josh to buy him out of the contracting business by 2031 while he keeps the farm and lambs.
S3.feel: Properly calm, the calm of having a good plan.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build something and sell it before the big boys catch up.
S3.fieldNote: Aaron neatly contrasts the warning times: two years means gambling with borrowed money, five means building with his own. His advice to older chapel farmers is to keep land in families and avoid selling to investment funds. He pictures keeping the lambs 'to potter with'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and anyone who's not ready by then hasn't tried. That sounds hard, but I'd say it. I'd also say the church and families should look after those who really can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'll be sixty-eight, Josh will have the business, and I'll have more time for the grandchildren and the lambs. The money's fine. My only thought is whether the early robots will be cheap enough by then that the contracting isn't worth much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the contracting slowly over the next few years, adding robots once they're proven and the price drops. I'd hand Josh the business around 2032 and keep the farm. And I'd put some savings into a couple of houses in the village to rent out, because people will still need somewhere to live whatever robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'll be a man with sheep, a pension and a son who runs robots. I can't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why houses, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can't see a robot building a house cheaper than people for a good while yet, and rents go up. It's old-fashioned, but old-fashioned works. And I'd rather rent to local families than to strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone not ready hasn't tried. Is that fair to everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Some folk are ill, or caring for someone, or just too old. That's what family and church are for. But most people, given ten years, can learn something. I did, at fifty-five.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, and anyone not ready by then hasn't tried. The church and families should look after those who really can't.
S4.think: For me it's comfortable: I'll be sixty-eight, Josh will have the business and the money's fine. My only thought is whether cheap robots will make the contracting worth little by then.
S4.do: Grows the contracting business slowly, adding robots once proven and cheaper. Hands it to Josh around 2032, keeps the farm and invests savings in a couple of village houses to rent to local families.
S4.quote: I'll be a man with sheep, a pension and a son who runs robots. I can't complain.
S4.fieldNote: Aaron is calm in every AGI picture; the warning time changes his risk, not his mood. When I asked whether 'hasn't tried' was fair, he softened and named illness, caring and age, but kept his view that family and church should carry those people. His property plan shows his trust in old-fashioned assets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, but more for the older men at chapel than for me. It'd be too quick for them. What would help is the government keeping out of the way of people starting businesses, more apprenticeships with the dealers, and rules that stop investment funds buying up family farms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what my father would think. He farmed with a horse till he was twenty. He'd have thought a tractor with a cab was the end of the world, and here's his son picking out robots on his phone. Every generation thinks the next one's lost the plot.

headlineQuote: He'd have thought a tractor with a cab was the end of the world, and here's his son picking out robots on his phone.
portrait: Aaron Costa, 58, grows sugar beet and barley, finishes lambs over winter, and runs a contracting business with his son Josh. He's chapel-going and traditional on family, free-market on the economy, and has used AI tools daily for three years. With land and solid savings capping his risk, he stays calm across every scenario and sees robots mainly as a contracting opportunity. Two years makes him gamble on borrowed money with a planned exit by 2031; five or ten let him build steadily, hand over to Josh and keep his lambs. His real worry is older friends at chapel who won't adapt.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mainly for the older farmers at chapel who'd have no time to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: Government keeping out of the way of people starting businesses, more apprenticeships with machinery dealers and rules stopping investment funds buying family farms.
